title: Search Foundations
description: Ten original questions on problem formulation, nodes, frontiers, reached sets, BFS, depth-limited search and iterative deepening. Multiple-response scoring is for practice only: +1 per correct selection and -0.5 per incorrect selection, floored at zero.

questions.prompt: Which elements belong in a standard search-problem formulation?

options.content: An initial state
A path-cost function when solution cost matters
A goal test
Available actions and a transition model
A hard-coded solution path

questions.explanation: A problem states where search begins, how states change, how success is recognized and how paths are evaluated. The solution is discovered by the algorithm and must not be embedded in the formulation.

questions.prompt: Why can two different search nodes contain the same state?

options.content: The nodes may have different parent links and depths.
A state necessarily stores the complete path history itself.
The state may be reached through different paths.
The nodes may have different path costs.

questions.explanation: A state describes a world configuration, whereas a node records one path to that state, including parent, action, depth and cost. Redundant paths can therefore create distinct nodes with the same state.

questions.prompt: For a finite-branching graph with unit step costs, which statements about breadth-first search are correct?

options.content: It expands nodes in nondecreasing depth.
It uses a FIFO frontier.
Its memory use is always linear in solution depth.
It is complete when a solution exists at finite depth.
It returns a minimum-step solution under unit costs.

questions.explanation: FIFO ordering produces layer-by-layer expansion, giving completeness and shortest path in number of steps under unit costs. BFS may store an entire frontier layer, so its memory can grow exponentially with depth.

questions.prompt: Under the Assignment 1 measurement convention, when is the goal test applied?

options.content: Immediately when a successor is generated
Only after the goal node has been expanded
When a node is removed from the frontier for processing
Only after the frontier becomes empty

questions.explanation: The assignment explicitly standardizes goal testing at removal from the frontier. This makes traces and popped-node counts comparable across implementations.

questions.prompt: What benefits can a reached structure provide in graph search?

options.content: It can prevent repeatedly expanding the same state through redundant paths.
For cost-based search, it can help track the cheapest known path to a state.
It can keep cycles from generating an endless sequence of repeated states.
It makes every heuristic search optimal regardless of frontier ordering.

questions.explanation: Reached-state bookkeeping controls repetition and may store the best known node for each state. It does not repair an unsuitable priority rule or automatically make a heuristic algorithm optimal.
questions.source: EE2213 EE2213_L03_search.pdf, page 3; EE2213 EE2213_Assignment1.pdf, pages 2-4

questions.prompt: A correct depth-limited search must distinguish which outcomes?

options.content: SOLUTION when a goal node is found
FAILURE when the finite search space is exhausted without a cutoff
CUT-OFF whenever the goal is absent, even if no node reaches the limit
CUT-OFF when at least one branch is stopped only by the depth limit

questions.explanation: CUT-OFF means the current limit may have hidden a deeper solution, whereas FAILURE means no solution exists in the explored finite space. IDS relies on this distinction to know whether increasing the limit can help.

questions.prompt: Which statements describe iterative deepening search (IDS) correctly?

options.content: It runs depth-limited search with limits $0,1,2,...$.
It should permanently mark every state reached in an earlier, shallower iteration.
With unit costs, it finds a shallowest solution like BFS.
Each iteration starts with fresh reached or path bookkeeping.

questions.explanation: IDS systematically increases the depth bound. Reusing a global reached set would wrongly block states that must be revisited with a larger remaining depth allowance. Its repeated shallow work is offset by depth-first memory use.

questions.prompt: In one DLS iteration, what does path-based cycle checking forbid?

options.content: Reaching a state that appeared anywhere in a different completed branch
Generating any node deeper than its parent
Generating the goal state
Generating a successor whose state already appears on the current node's ancestor path

questions.explanation: Path checking prevents a branch from looping back to one of its own ancestors while still allowing the same state to be explored through a different path. That is less restrictive than a global reached set.

questions.prompt: BFS uses FIFO, goal-on-pop, and reached-on-generation including S. Successors are `S:[A,B]`, `A:[C,D]`, `B:[D]`, `C:[]`, `D:[G]`, `G:[]`, in that order. Which trace statements are correct?

options.content: Expanding B does not add a second D.
The processed pop sequence is S,A,B,C,D,G (six nodes).
The maximum frontier size is four.
The returned parent-chain path is S-B-D-G.
Immediately after expanding A, the frontier is [B,C,D].

questions.explanation: S inserts A,B. A then inserts C,D, yielding [B,C,D], the peak size 3. D is already reached when B generates it, so no duplicate is inserted. The path is S-A-D-G, because A discovered D first. Goal-on-pop includes G in the six-node count.
questions.source: EE2213 EE2213_L03_search.pdf, page 3; EE2213 EE2213_Assignment1.pdf, page 2

questions.prompt: Under the Assignment 1 convention, maximum frontier size excludes the initial frontier and is measured before adding the successors of each expansion.

options.content: True
False

questions.explanation: False. The specified measurement includes the initial frontier and samples size after all insertions or updates due to an expansion. Measuring before successors are added can miss the maximum and makes the reported count inconsistent with the assignment.
